title: What Is Monitored Containment? — Operational Deployment Guide (Council of AI, 2026-10-07)
context: 2026-10-07 EAT cycle — third consecutive pod-unreachable cycle; this seed focuses on the operational deployment path: how a compliance officer or deployer operationalises monitored containment in a live environment, distinct from the definitional seed of 2026-10-03.
body: Monitored containment is not a compliance checkbox — it is an operational posture. The question most deployers ask is not 'what is it?' but 'how do I run it?' The answer has four operational layers. Layer 1: measurement surface definition. Before any monitoring begins, the deployer selects which axes are relevant to their risk profile. The Council of AI's 14-axis board (detection, care, denial, governance, provenance, adversarial resilience, privacy, and seven others) is a reference set, not a mandate — a healthcare deployer may weight care and privacy heavier than a financial institution that weights detection and denial. The point is that the axis selection is explicit, documented, and frozen into the manifest before measurement begins. Layer 2: signed baseline. The initial board state is captured in an Ed25519-signed manifest. This manifest is the deployer's canonical reference: every subsequent measurement is compared against it, and drift is flagged. The signing ensures that no one — not the deployer, not the platform vendor, not the auditor — can retroactively alter the baseline. Layer 3: continuous measurement cadence. Monitored containment requires that measurements are taken at a defined cadence (daily for high-frequency systems, weekly for stable deployments). Each measurement produces a signed capsule that records the axis value, the model version, the input distribution sample, and the timestamp. These capsules accumulate into an append-only log. Layer 4: credential issuance. When a third party requests evidence of containment posture, the deployer issues a verified measurement credential — a signed object that binds a specific board state to a specific time window. The credential is not a 'compliance certificate' in the traditional sense; it is a frozen, verifiable snapshot that the recipient can check against the public manifest. The critical distinction from traditional compliance: monitored containment does not claim the system is safe. It claims that the system's risk posture has been continuously measured against a defined reference, that the measurements are signed, and that the record is auditable. This is monitored containment, not provable isolation. A deployer who tells their board 'our AI is safe because we have a measurement framework' has misunderstood the concept. The framework says: 'here is what we measured, here is the signed record, here is the drift since baseline — judge for yourself.' That honesty is the operational value.
